description:
Your Land. Your Legacy. Our Mission.

We stand for those who have cultivated, protected, and lived alongside the land for generations. From farmers sustaining our future to Indigenous communities preserving generations of knowledge, our mission is to turn intelligence from the skies into resilience on the ground.
summary: Modern farming is becoming increasingly complex, since farmers must interpret vast amounts of environmental data and predict unpredictable conditions through a complex interface. A study of 37.1% of farmers found uncertainty about how to apply systemic data to their agricultural decisions, “highlighting a need for more practical, user-friendly tailored broadcasts” (SpringerNature, 2025). The fundamental challenge is not the lack of agricultural data – it is the gap between complex environmental information and farmers’ ability to turn it into timely, informed decisions. As a result, we decided to create an interactive, gamified simulation that transforms environmental data into a hands-on learning experience. Farmers will learn different considerations that integrate NASA data in real time to manage their farms against environmental conditions. Our project operates through a three-dimensional simulation of agricultural environments, where farmers will have to: manage irrigation systems, which represent the underground layer; monitor soil moisture, which represents the ground layer; and implement cover crops, which protect the soil against environmental threats from the sky. Of course, we will have unpredictable scenarios that integrate real-world scenarios, where farmers will have to make brisk decisions to preserve their agriculture.
details:
Field Shift works within the Lower Fraser Valley, spanning Richmond, Delta (including Ladner), Langley and Abbotsford. Each municipality has distinct agricultural industries and crop varieties. Richmond is particularly known for cranberries and blueberries, alongside Chinese cabbage and other field vegetables. Delta and Ladner have extensive potato and vegetable production, including cabbage, greenhouse tomatoes, sweet peppers and cucumbers, as well as blueberries, cranberries and forage crops. Langley supports a diverse agricultural industry, including blueberries, cranberries, raspberries, strawberries, grapes, greenhouse vegetables and dairy farming. Abbotsford is a major agricultural centre for blueberries and raspberries, alongside hay, forage, pasture, vegetables, dairy and poultry production. These different farming systems face environmental challenges associated with changing rainfall, water availability, soil moisture and temperature, making the region an ideal setting for exploring climate-resilient agriculture.

In our game (Defend Your Farm), we use 6 different datasets from NASA to produce varied and geographically accurate scenarios for players to farm in. Instead of populating these scenarios with arbitrary dangers, we utilize NASA POWER. For each player's chosen region, we obtain a day-by-day record over 1 year covering: air temperature, rainfall, wind, relative humidity and root zone soil moisture. These will be used to set the game's weather, environment, threats and level progression on a week-to-week basis.

A further five NASA data sets form the underpinning of these threat scenarios: SMAP is used to determine drought via root zone soil moisture, GPM IMERG to drive flood risk, MODIS and VIIRS return NDVI to indicate levels of crop and bare ground vulnerability, Landsat 8 and 9 deliver 30m resolution to probe individual fields and finally ECOSTRESS enables us to model the threat from high temperatures using surface temperature and ET.

In addition to helping farmers cope with a changing climate, Field Shift has the potential to consider agriculture's role in generating greenhouse gases. Livestock produce methane (CH₄), fertilisers give rise to nitrous oxide (N₂O), and fossil fuels and disturbance of organic carbon in the soil result in CO₂. Players could therefore need to manage their use of fertilizer, water, manures and inter-cropping to minimize their impact. Based on data from each individual farm, emissions could then be calculated and shown to decrease through adoption of various measures including increased soil carbon sequestration. Data from NASA may be incorporated into the game to allow the player to consider wider climatic effects, with a distinct model applied to predict the farm's GHG output.

Field Shift will include an additional layer regarding the nutrients present in the farm's soil. Nitrogen, Phosphorus and Potassium (NPK) will be key to the gameplay, allowing players to learn about and manage these elements required for above and below ground plant biomass, carbon fixation and control of soil water content. As with any farming game, Field Shift will require players to have sufficient NPK in their fields through means including but not limited to if ethical: addition of organic matter, intercropping, green manure and commercial fertilizers. Over-fertilizing will result in loss of nutrients to the wider environment, local water bodies may degrade and CO2 emissions may increase (from NOx generated by N inputs). When paired with real-world data from NASA on precipitation, soil wetness and NDVI, Defend Your Farm can show players the true impact that external factors have on their farmed soils.

In essence, this gives Defend Your Farm the ability to depict phenomena including drought, extreme flooding, hot spells and periods of poor plant health. It will be up to players to grow suitable crops, apply cover-crops, irrigate and modify their agricultural practices to overcome these events. Through doing so, Field Shift allows the public to engage with and learn from actual NASA data in relation to food production and our environment.

Functionality. Defend Your Farm is a browser game. The player sets a starting budget, a water allocation and a farm location, then plays six stages on a 3D field of five rows by eight plots. Each in-game day replays one real day of NASA POWER weather; drought, heat, wind, waterlogging, pests and frost hit every plot at once, and a crop loses health depending on its plot’s soil water, cover and shelter. The player places crops to earn money at harvest and farming practices to protect them. Each plot has four layers: underground (drip lines, drainage tile), ground (crops, windbreaks, companion marigolds), soil surface (mulch, cover crops) and sky (hoop covers). An in-game farming manual explains every hazard, every crop and practice, the NASA datasets behind them, how the simulation works and the crop rotation rules. The final stage opens a rotation planner: five rows by four seasons, priced against the budget, with a per-row analysis of what the rotation will do to yield and pests and an estimate of each season’s irrigation need against the water allocation. The year then plays out over 52 weeks of real weather.

Mechanism. On setup the game requests one calendar year of NASA POWER daily data for the chosen coordinates: air temperature, daily maximum and minimum, precipitation, wind speed and direction, relative humidity and root-zone soil wetness. It aggregates the 365 days into 52 weeks and converts each week into six hazard indices, blending agronomic thresholds (rain under 5 mm, highs above 28 °C, a minimum below 0 °C, more than 30 mm in a week) with the location’s own range, so every farm has a real dry season and a real wet season. For each stage the game scans the year’s growing-season weeks for the window where that stage’s hazard index is highest, so the drought stage plays in the location’s driest weeks and the flood stage in its wettest. Each day every plot runs a soil water balance (rain in, minus runoff; FAO-56 Hargreaves evapotranspiration out), and the day’s maximum, minimum, wind and humidity decide heat, frost, erosion and pest damage against each crop’s own thresholds; rain partly refills the farm pond and drip lines draw from it. Practices either serve the whole row (drip irrigation, drainage tile), shelter nearby plots (windbreaks, marigolds) or protect one plot (mulch, cover crops, hoop covers), and each one answers only the hazards it would answer in a real field. Rotation rules apply at each season change: the same crop family twice triples starting pests, makes them arrive 1.8 times faster and cuts yield by 15%, a legume before any other crop raises yield by 25%, a cover crop before a cash crop lets the soil hold 15% more water and raises yield by 10%. If NASA POWER cannot be reached, the game falls back to a built-in latitude-aware climatology and labels the data source on screen as offline.

Benefits. The player never reads a chart; they lose a tomato crop to a heatwave the day after the 7-day forecast shows a heat icon, and next time they put up a hoop cover first. The link from a NASA measurement (soil wetness, daily rainfall, daily maximum) to a farm decision (irrigate, drain, shade) is the whole game loop, repeated every in-game day (1.25 seconds at normal speed). Because the data is fetched live for any coordinates, the same build works for any region without a content team. The budget and water constraints make the trade-offs the ones a farmer actually faces: drip irrigation stops droughts but spends the allocation; tomatoes pay most and die first.

Objectives. Make NASA Earth-observation data legible to the people who most need it, in the form they are least likely to reject: a game you can finish in twenty minutes. Teach six climate threats, seven adaptation practices and the logic of crop rotation. Give agricultural educators a free, no-install tool that uses the learner’s own region.

Technology. Vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step. Three.js r128 renders the 3D field at 30% resolution and upscales it with nearest-neighbour sampling, so it reads as pixel art while remaining a real 3D scene with an underground layer the player can X-ray. All icons, including the farmer guide, are hand-authored pixel maps (12 by 12, the farmer 16 by 24) rendered to canvas at runtime, so the game ships no image assets. Data comes from the NASA POWER API (agriculture community, daily point endpoint, no API key). Threat design is modelled on SMAP, GPM IMERG, MODIS NDVI, Landsat and ECOSTRESS. Fonts are Press Start 2P and VT323. The whole game is seven source files and runs from any static host.
